Plan this as a Rhylthyme protocol and deliver a live timeline: Passaging Two Flasks of Adherent HEK293 Cells for two T75 flasks split 1:6 into four
Resource limits: one biosafety cabinet, one 37 °C water bath, one CO₂ incubator, one benchtop centrifuge, one microscope with haemocytometer, one operator.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Passaging Two Flasks of Adherent HEK293 Cells

Two T75 flasks at about 90 % confluence are split 1:6 into four new flasks. The room has one biosafety cabinet, one 37 °C water bath, one CO₂ incubator, one benchtop centrifuge and one microscope with a haemocytometer. Only one flask can be open in the cabinet at a time, so the two flasks queue for it while the centrifuge and the microscope stay free. Work with pre-warmed medium, PBS and trypsin-EDTA throughout; nothing cold touches the cells. One operator.

Preparation
1. Wipe down the cabinet, lay out pipettes and tubes, and let the blower run; 10 minutes.
2. Check both flasks on the microscope for confluence and contamination; 10 minutes.

Flask A
3. Aspirate the spent medium and rinse the monolayer with 5 mL of PBS; 4 minutes in the cabinet.
4. Add 2 mL of trypsin-EDTA, rock the flask and return it to the incubator for 5 minutes.
5. Knock the flask, check detachment and neutralise with 8 mL of medium; 5 minutes in the cabinet.
6. Transfer the suspension to a 15 mL tube and spin at 300 × g for 5 minutes.
7. Aspirate the supernatant and resuspend the pellet in 10 mL of fresh medium; 4 minutes.
8. Count the cells on the haemocytometer; 6 minutes.
9. Seed two new T75 flasks at 1:6 and label them; 6 minutes in the cabinet.
10. Return the new flasks to the incubator and leave them to settle overnight, at least 16 hours.

Flask B
11. Start flask B the moment flask A leaves the cabinet: aspirate and rinse with 5 mL of PBS; 4 minutes.
12. Trypsinise flask B in the incubator for 5 minutes.
13. Neutralise flask B as soon as flask A is out of the cabinet again; 5 minutes.
14. Spin flask B at 300 × g for 5 minutes once the centrifuge is free.
15. Resuspend the flask B pellet in 10 mL of fresh medium; 4 minutes.
16. Count flask B on the haemocytometer once flask A has been counted; 6 minutes.
17. Seed two more T75 flasks at 1:6 and label them; 6 minutes.
18. Return them to the incubator to settle overnight alongside the first pair.

Finishing
19. Wipe the cabinet down, discard the waste and switch the blower to standby; 10 minutes.
20. Write the passage number, the split ratio and the counts into the culture log; 5 minutes.
>>>

This protocol passages two T75 flasks of adherent HEK293 cells (currently ~90% confluent) at a 1:6 split ratio, producing four new T75 flasks total (two from each original flask), which are then left to settle in the incubator overnight (at least 16 hours) before the process is complete with a final cabinet cleanup and log entry. There is no external deadline — the work should finish as early as possible given the constraints. The single operator must work flask A and flask B through a shared sequence of steps, queuing for the one biosafety cabinet (only one flask open in it at a time — this is the key bottleneck driving the interleaving of A and B), while also sharing a single 37 °C water bath, one CO₂ incubator, one benchtop centrifuge, and one microscope with haemocytometer. Flask B's cabinet steps are explicitly timed to start as soon as flask A vacates the cabinet, and flask B's cell count must wait until flask A's count is done (microscope contention), while the centrifuge step for B waits for the centrifuge to free up after A's spin. All reagents (medium, PBS, trypsin-EDTA) are kept pre-warmed throughout, meaning no explicit warming/holding step is needed but nothing cold should touch the cells. The overnight settling period (≥16 hours) for both flask pairs is the long tail of the schedule, after which a final cabinet wipe-down and culture log entry close out the protocol.

A **track** represents one continuous line of work for a single flask (or for the whole operator when nothing else is running); steps inside a track are strictly sequential and must never overlap in time, so anything that happens concurrently with another step — flask B's cabinet work while flask A's suspension is spinning, say — needs its own separate track. Each **step** carries exactly one duration shape: `fixed` when the time is a fixed number of seconds, `variable` when it ranges between a min and max (with a default for planning), or `indefinite` when the person decides when it ends. A **startTrigger** is what actually places a step on the clock, either anchored to programStart/programStartOffset or chained to another step's end (or start, with a buffer) via `afterStep`/`afterStepWithBuffer`, or left to a manual tap or a compound condition; this is how flask B's steps get tied to flask A vacating the cabinet. `stepId` values must be unique across the entire program, not just within a track, since triggers reference them globally. Every distinct `task` string that a step occupies (cabinet, incubator, centrifuge, microscope) needs exactly one matching `resourceConstraints` entry whose `maxConcurrent` enforces the real-world exclusivity — that's what will force flask B to literally wait for the cabinet or the centrifuge instead of running in parallel. Since nothing here repeats identically n times in a way that needs `replicates` (flask A and flask B differ enough in their triggers to be modeled as two explicit tracks rather than one replicated step), I don't expect to need `replicates`/`maxInFlight` for this protocol.

- one operator throughout (actors: 1); the water bath is used only to keep reagents pre-warmed in the background and isn't occupied by any explicit step, so I don't plan to give it a task/resourceConstraint.

Turn 4 of 4 — relationships, then the program.

Take the step list from turn 3 exactly as it stands.

**First, tracks.** Put each step in a track: one track per parallel line of work — per dish, per station, per instrument, per performer, per sample group. Steps in one track run one after another and must not overlap; anything that runs while something else runs belongs in its own track.

**Second, triggers.** Give every step a `startTrigger` from this vocabulary and no other:

- `{"type":"programStart"}` — at t = 0.
- `{"type":"programStartOffset","offsetSeconds":n}` — n seconds after the start; this is how a short track is delayed so it finishes with the others.
- `{"type":"afterStep","stepId":"x"}` — when x ends. Add `"offsetSeconds"` for a gap, `"event":"start"` to hang off x's start instead of its end, `"instances"` when x is replicated.
- `{"type":"afterStepWithBuffer","stepId":"x","bufferSeconds":n}` — n seconds after x ends.
- `{"type":"manual"}` — the person taps to start it: a gate that no clock can predict (guests seated, dough looks right, the surgeon is ready).
- `{"type":"compound","logic":"all"|"any","triggers":[...]}` — wait for all of, or the first of, several triggers.

**Third, refine the question before you answer it.** Within the scope of scheduling these activities for one person to follow, suggest a better version of the question "which activities depend on which, and which can run at the same time?" — one that would expose dependencies this text implies but does not state: things that must cool, rest, preheat, thaw, proof, be held warm, or be ready at the same moment as something else. 2. Otherwise keep the program you just built; `rhylthyme://guide/authoring` is the cheat-sheet and `rhylthyme://examples/*` are complete programs to pattern-match.
